post_text:
I pinned our JVM heap limits to 65% of the container memory and set requests equal to limits.

The platform team hated the wasted overhead, and for months, I worried I had over-provisioned out of sheer paranoia.

Everyone wanted tight bin-packing on our Kubernetes nodes, arguing that modern G1GC ergonomics made safety buffers obsolete.

I held my ground anyway, terrified that off-heap allocations, Metaspace growth, and thread stacks would invite the Linux OOM killer before the garbage collector could even react.

Six months later, an external SDK update introduced a silent direct-memory leak during our peak traffic window.

Neighboring microservices dropped instantly in unlogged OOM-kill loops, but our pods absorbed the native buffer bloat and gave us two calm hours to route traffic away.

Nobody celebrated because nothing visibly broke. It simply looked like ordinary stability, confirming my suspicion that surviving production often comes down to deliberately unoptimized margins.

What I learned:

Leaving unallocated headroom inside a container is not wasted spend, but the cheapest insurance against runtime unpredictability.
